The maximum launch wet mass is 242 Kg and can include up to 45 Kg of payload depending on AV needs. The on-board propulsion system is used for maneuvering hi the Earth-Moon system and injecting the spacecraft into its final orbit or trajectory. For Mars missions, MSC enables orbiting Mars for science payloads and/or communications and navigation assets, or for precision Mars fly-bys to drop up to six probes. The micromissions spacecraft bus can be used for science targets other than Mars, including the Moon, Earth, Venus, Earth-Sun Lagrange points, or other small bodies. This paper summarizes the current spacecraft concept and describes the multimission spacecraft bus implementation in more detail. © 2006 IEEE.

Authors: Piva S.; Zara M.; Gera G.; Regazzoni C.S.
Title: Color-based video stabilization for real-time on-board object detection on high-speed trains
Source title: Proceedings - IEEE Conference on Advanced Video and Signal Based Surveillance, AVSS 2003
Abstract: This paper is concerned with a particular application of image stabilization. Image stabilization is a necessary step to reduce the effect of camera motion when, as in this case, image sequences are acquired from a mobile platform. In this work, in order to find an efficient motion estimator, two one-dimensional characteristic curves are extracted from each video frame. Such curves are then compared in consequent frames to estimate image displacement. The proposed algorithm is suitable for real time processing and provides good performance; in order to verify its validity, it has been tested on a variety of color video-sequences taken from the point of view of trains moving along railways tracks. Results are provided in order to compare the proposed approach with a feature-based stabilization method. © 2003 IEEE.
Author Keywords: Cameras; Color; Image sequences; Layout; Motion compensation; Motion estimation; Object detection; Rail transportation; Real time systems; Testing

Authors: Kagami S.; Nishiwaki K.; Sugihara T.; Kuffner J.J. Jr.; Inaba M.; Inoue H.
Title: Design and implementation of software research platform for humanoid robotics: H6
Source title: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation
Abstract: A humanoid robot "H6" is developed as a platform for the research on perception-action coupling in intelligent behaviour of humanoid type robots. The H6 has the features as follows: 1) body which has enough DOFs and each joint has enough torque for full body motion. 2) PC/AT compatible high-performance on-board computer which is controlled by RT-linux so that from low-level to high-level control is achieved simultaneously.3) self-contained and connected to a network via radio ethernet.4) Dynamic walking trajectory generation, motion planning and 3D vision functions are available. The H6 is expected to be a common test-bed in experiment and discussion for various aspects of intelligent humanoid robotics.

Authors: Würflinger K.; Kubesch P.; Maurutschek P.
Author full names: Würflinger, K. (6505972719); Kubesch, P. (6603193238); Maurutschek, P. (6506956460)
Title: Mamba - a programmable broadband multimedia interface board
Source title: IEEE International Performance, Computing and Communications Conference, Proceedings
Abstract: The document on hand describes a design approach and a hardware implementation sketch for a high speed interface card1, capable of transmitting and receiving 216 MBit/sec raw DVB/ATSC data via Asynchronous Serial or Synchronous Parallel Interface (ASI/SPI). Local side interface is CompactPCI (CPCI). On-board performance bottlenecks will be largely avoided by utilising the new Zero Bus Turnaround RAM technology as primary buffer memory along with a sophisticated state-of-the-art buffer management system. A commonly used processor from Intel, often found in nowadays embedded systems, builds the processing core of the system, running a lean real-time operating system for optimal performance gain. Full software configuration possibilities makes this hardware design most flexible for a wide variety of applications. Mechanical and electrical constraints like HotSwap capability, given by the CPCI standard, make the hardware robust enough for nearly all operation environments and fail-safe through redundant setup potential.

Authors: Neale R.
Title: Motorola aims the VME bus for a future as good as the past
Source title: Electronic Engineering (London)
Abstract: Motorola believes that the ability to evolve with backward compatibility will be an essential feature of future success with further development of the VME bus. Part of that faith in the future evolution of the VMEbus is the recent announcement of a new chip called "Tempe" that acts as an interface to the new next generation high speed 2eSST specification.

Authors: Hsiung S.; Willis J.
Author full names: Hsiung, Steve (7005649278); Willis, Jeff (16641071300)
Title: A new approach in microprocessor/microcontrollercourses/laboratories material design and development
Source title: ASEE Annual Conference and Exposition, Conference Proceedings
Abstract: Courses in microprocessors and microcontrollers are standard parts of the Engineering Technology core curricula. The traditional course material developments include both lectures and associated laboratory exercises. No matter how creative is the curriculum; it is usually budgetary constraints that confine the creativity when developing new curricula. This limits the freedom of the major approach in new course development. This article demonstrates new course lecture and laboratories material development that starts from ground up with both a hardware platform and simulation software design for microprocessor/microcontroller related courses. It is not only very cost effective, but also does not limit the instructor's creativity when developing new curricula. The only obstacle is the instructor's imagination on courses and laboratories activities. This system can be implemented at no cost to the department for sponsoring the courses. As a matter of fact, the initial trials of this system have generated revenue, thereby supporting future improvements and development needs. This new approach in course improvement starts with the design of a hardware platform in a custom made evaluation board. It involves the system circuit and power supply design, printed circuit board layout, prototype testing, and circuit board fabrication. The second step is to design the simulation software for laboratory uses. The total design and development of both software and hardware was a two year evolutionary process. © American Society for Engineering Education, 2006.

Authors: He C.; Zhao W.; Lu M.
Title: FPGA-based high-order finite difference algorithm for 2D acoustic wave propagation problems
Source title: Proceedings of the 2005 International Conference on Engineering of Reconfigurable Systems and Algorithms, ERSA'05
Abstract: Finite Difference Time Domain (FDTD) method is the most commonly used numerical algorithm for simulating linear wave propagation phenomena in geophysics, electromagnetics, and aero- or marine-acoustics applications. Unfortunately, evaluating time-evolution for millions to trillions of discrete spatial points is computational intensive, especially when the geometrical size under study is much larger than the wavelength of excitations or long time integration is needed. In this paper, we proposed an FPGA-based hardware implementation to accelerate these simulation tasks. By adopting high-order temporal and spatial finite difference numerical algorithms along with efficient on-chip memory architecture, we alleviate the bandwidth bottleneck between the FPGA chip and onboard memories at the cost of increased computational burdens, which are absorbed effectively into the pipelined computing engine without speed penalty. The speed of our design implemented on Xilinx ML401 Virtex-4 evaluation platform is about 7∼20 times faster than a pure software implementation of the same algorithm running on a 3.0GHz DELL workstation. Moreover, the desirable properties of simplicity and scalability make our design compatible with most commercial reconfigurable coprocessor platforms and correspondingly, the performance would be proportional to their available onboard memory bandwidth.

Authors: Kohli I.
Author full names: Kohli, Inder (6603274097)
Title: PCI express powers machine vision
Source title: EE: Evaluation Engineering
Abstract: PCI Express (PCIe) is the next-generation peripheral bus that provides a scalable, high-bandwidth, point-to-point pathway between peripheral cards and computing core. The serial PCIe bus, using a switch matrix, can make point-to-point connections to provide a direct, bidirectional link between the two communicating entities. The design of a peripheral card for a PCIe system can use either a bridge or a native interface, and it is possible to connect an existing PCI or PCI-X design to a PCIe slot through a bridge chip, because of a software compatibility. The native PCIe interface enable users to address a wide variety of machine vision applications. A PCIe-based system can use multiple frame grabber boards and provide each with an independent link to system memory. The bidirectional capability of the PCIe can help in simplifying the use of coprocessors to enhance the future machine vision systems performance.

Authors: Hsivng S.C.; Ward D.A.
Author full names: Hsivng, Steve C. (36713540600); Ward, Dave A. (55464704500)
Title: Designing software and hardware for PC I/O control
Source title: Journal of Engineering Technology
Abstract: The lienor PC operating systems, such as Windows NT/2000/XP, are based on the Windows NT platform, which is quite different from Windows 95/98 that was based on the DOS platform. The NT platform puts the PC's CPU in protected mode, and makes input/output (I/O) difficult. These changes also affect the software needed to control I/O ports like the parallel/printer port. This article demonstrates the use of a readily available free I/O software driver 1 tbat can be easily accessed from Microsoft Visual Basic 6.0 (VB6) 1.3 and Visual C++. 5- The application of the software is made on a cost-effective interfacing hardware design, including a printed circuit board (PCB) layout that allows I/O through a typical PC's parallel/printer port. 2.3 A direct interface between a PC and any external control circuit is not recommended. It is strongly suggested that there be an electronic protection between these two devices to prevent any electrical damage. 2 This article also addresses ways to electrically protect the PC in the I/O controlling applications.

Authors: Park H.; Friedman J.; Srivastava M.B.; Burke J.
Author full names: Park, Heemin (60396990100); Friedman, Jonathan (55253137700); Srivastava, Mani B. (35599699800); Burke, Jeff (9042957400)
Title: A new light sensing module for Mica motes
Source title: Proceedings of IEEE Sensors
Abstract: We present the Dlumimote, a new light sensing module for the Mica mote platform. The Illumimote achieves performance comparable to a commercial light intensity meter, while conforming to the size and energy constraints imposed by its application in wireless sensor networks. The Illumimote was developed to replace the Mica sensor board (MTS310) whose slow response time and narrow dynamic range in light intensity capture is unsuitable to many applications, including media production. The Illumimote features significantly improved SNR due to its adoption of high-end photo sensors, amplification and conversion circuits coupled with active noise suppression, application-tuned filter networks, and a noise-attentive manual layout. Unlike the MTS310, the Illumimote can capture RGB color intensity (for color temperature calculation) and incident light angle (which discerns the angle of ray arrival from the strongest source). Our prototype demonstrated significantly faster response time (> 6x) and a much wider dynamic range (> 10x) in light intensity measurement as compared with the MTS310. The light-angle estimation results were well correlated with an average error of just 2.63°. © 2005 IEEE.

Authors: See K.Y.; Liu Z.H.; Li E.P.
Title: MoM modeling of high-speed power bus radiation
Source title: Proceedings of 6th Electronics Packaging Technology Conference, EPTC 2004
Abstract: Conventional method of moments (MoM) simulation tools assume printed circuit structure with circuit traces backed by infinite substrate and ground plane [1]. These tools have the inherent limitation to model realistic finitesize power bus structure. A surface-volume integral equation formulation solved by MoM is proposed to overcome this limitation. The proposed MoM simulation code allows modeling of radiation from realistic finite-size power bus structure. It also has the flexibility to handle ground discontinuity, such as slots and holes in the ground plane. Some simulation results are shown to demonstrate these flexible features of the MoM code. © 2004 IEEE.

Authors: Schoenauer T.; Atasoy S.; Mehrtash N.; Klar H.
Title: Simulation of a digital neuro-chip for spiking neural networks
Source title: Proceedings of the International Joint Conference on Neural Networks
Abstract: Conventional hardware platforms are far from reaching real-time simulation requirements of complex spiking neural networks (SNN). Therefore we designed an accelerator board with a neuro-processor-chip, called NeuroPipe-Chip. In this paper, we introduce two new concepts on chip-level to speed up the simulation of SNN. The concepts are implemented in the architecture of the NeuroPipe-Chip. We present the hardware structure of the NeuroPipe-Chip, which is modelled on register-transfer-level (RTL) using the hardware description language VHDL. We evaluate the performance of the NeuroPipe-Chip in a system simulation, where the rest of the accelerator board is modelled in behavioral VHDL. For a simple SNN for image segmentation, the NeuroPipe-Chip operating at 100 MHz shows an improvement of more than two orders of magnitude compared to an Alpha 500 MHz workstation and approaches real-time requirements for SNN in the order of 106 neurons. Hence, such an accelerator would allow real-time simulations of complex SNN for image processing. Currently, the implementation of the NeuroPipe-Chip in a 0.35 m digital CMOS technology is investigated.

Authors: Do Carmo Lucas A.; Heithecker S.; Rüffer P.; Ernst R.; Rückert H.; Wischermann G.; Gebel K.; Fach R.; Huther W.; Eichner S.; Scheller G.
Author full names: Do Carmo Lucas, Amilcar (8950139900); Heithecker, Sven (9338144800); Rüffer, Peter (6507814034); Ernst, Rolf (7201529254); Rückert, Holger (16176087700); Wischermann, Gerhard (7801440458); Gebel, Karin (54893076700); Fach, Reinhard (57217929861); Huther, Wolfgang (6602138703); Eichner, Stefan (6603414788); Scheller, Gunter (7003457695)
Title: A reconfigurable HW/SW platform for computation intensive high-resolution real-time digital film applications
Source title: Proceedings -Design, Automation and Test in Europe, DATE
Abstract: This paper presents a multi-board, multi-FPGA hardware/software architecture, for computation intensive, high resolution (2048×2048 pixels), real-time (24 frames per second) digital film processing. It is based on Xilinx Virtex-II Pro FPGAs, large SDRAM memories for multiple frame storage and a PCI express communication network. The architecture reaches record performance running a complex noise reduction algorithm including a 2.5 dimensions DWT and a full 16×16 motion estimation at 24 fps requiring a total of 203 Gops/s net computing performance and a total of 28 Gbit/s DDR-SDRAM frame memory bandwidth. To increase design productivity and yet achieve high clock rates (125MHz), the architecture combines macro component configuration and macro level floorplanning with weak programmability using distributed microcoding. As an example, the core of the bidirectional motion estimation using 2772 CLBs reaching 155 Gop/s (1538 op/pixel) requiring 7 Gbit/s external memory bandwidth was developed in two men-months.
Author Keywords: Digital film; FPGA; Motion-estimation; Reconfigurable; Stream-based architechture; Weak-programming

Authors: Nagatani T.; Yoshimura J.
Author full names: Nagatani, Takashi (7103106117); Yoshimura, Jin (7005207850)
Title: Dynamical transition in a coupled-map lattice model of a recurrent bus
Source title: Physica A: Statistical Mechanics and its Applications
Abstract: We investigate the dynamical behavior of a recurrent bus on a cyclic route with many bus stops. The maximum capacity of the bus is taken into account to study the dynamics of a waiting queue at a bus stop. We build a coupled-map lattice model of a cyclic bus. The recurrence time (one period) on each bus stop depends on the number M of bus stops, the maximum capacity Wmax of the bus, and the stopping time for new passengers to board the bus. The coupled-map lattice of all bus stops is approximated with a single nonlinear map of the average of all the stops. It is shown that the dynamical phase transition between the queuing and schedule-time phases occurs with varying the initial period. When the initial period is higher than a critical value, some persons waiting at a bus stop may not be able to board the bus because the bus is full. The waiting line at each bus stop increases with time, forming a queue. In contrast, if the initial period is less than the critical value, all waiting people at a bus stop can board the bus since the bus is not full. By selecting the combination of the number of bus stops, the maximum capacity of the bus and the initial period, one can operate the bus on a scheduled time without queues for an infinite time. © 2002 Elsevier Science B.V. All rights reserved.
Author Keywords: Coupled-map lattice; Cyclic bus; Dynamical transition

Authors: Ameli F.; Bonori M.
Title: The NEMO floor control module
Source title: IEEE Transactions on Nuclear Science
Abstract: An electronic board, called floor control module (FCM), was developed for the NEMO project, an underwater neutrino telescope. The offshore FCM Is In charge of providing Interfaces toward Instrumental control boards, collecting data from up to eight readout channels, packing and sending streams to the onshore laboratory through an optical fiber driven by a dense wavelength division multiplexing (DWDM) electro-optical transceiver. To obtain a common timing at each level of the apparatus, communication adopts the synchronous digital hierarchy (SDH) protocol, a standard telecommunication synchronous format which allows clock recovery from bitstream, thus simplifying the distribution network. The channel Is fully bidirectional to allow underwater apparatus control. The same FCM, plugged Into a PCI bus, can also be used onshore for data reception and transmission. This architecture provides a complete real-time data transport layer between the onshore laboratory and the underwater detector. © 2006 IEEE.
Author Keywords: DWDM; NEMO; Readout electronics; SDH

Authors: Rubenstein R.
Author full names: Rubenstein, Roy (7004403025)
Title: Making a connection
Source title: New Electronics
Abstract: Ethernet is playing an important role in providing the need for cost effective and efficient transport in connection based network schemes. Provider Backbone Technology (PBT) and Transport Multi Protocol Label Switching (T-MPLS), two new connection schemes, based on Ethernet are gaining importance. Danish start up TRACK has developed integrated packet processing and traffic management technology which supports both these protocols. TRACK is providing PBT and T-MPLS reference boards and fpga designs to vendors who are interested to add carrier Ethernet to their networking platforms. Spanning Tree and broad-casting, for PBT, are switched off, while for T-MPLS, a hopping scheme normally used to lessen the packet load is disabled, as is an MPLS scheme which gives packets the same label for data rerouting. This results a bidirectional point to point link which can be monitored by the carrier and which can be restored in 50 ms if a link element go down.

Authors: Libsch F.R.; Budd R.; Chiniwalla P.; Hobbs P.C.D.; Mastro M.; Sanford J.L.; Xu J.
Title: MCM LGA package with optical I/O passively aligned to dual layer polymer waveguides in PCB
Source title: Proceedings - Electronic Components and Technology Conference
Abstract: Over the past 30 years, IBM has provided leadership in high density I/O density and count interconnects at both chip and package levels as has been necessary for processor chips in high end symmetrical multiple processor (SMP) servers. For example, IBM introduced multi-chip modules (MCMs) in the 1970's, thermal conduction modules (TCMs) in the 1980's, and advanced organic micro-via buildup-layer packages in the 1990's [11]. Typically, MCMs are necessary to provide significant increases in bandwidth between chips on the module, compared to the alternative route of lower bandwidth resulting from chip-to-chip interconnects going through the printed circuit board (PCB) for single chip modules (SCMs). CMOS chip-to-package pad scaling gap has been growing compared to the package-to-printed circuit board (PCB) pad scaling, which is the reason for the I/O advantage of MCMs vs. SCMs. For example, today's mainstream IC-to-package flipchip bonding uses 0.1 mm square pads on 0.2 mm pitch, with 0.15 mm ramping up, while the package-to-PCB ball- or land grid array (BGA or LGA) pitch uses 1-mm pitch, an areal density as much as 64 times lower. However, even with the larger bandwidth advantage of MCMs, more complex chips such as multi-processor cores and the need for higher bandwidth to memory cache will require a relatively larger number of signal I/Os, as well as more power and ground I/Os. Faster I/O clocks will further exacerbate the need for more package I/O by forcing the transition from previous single-ended I/Os to differential signal I/Os to satisfy the higher frequency bit error rate specifications on SMP buses. Our goal is to alleviate the I/O bottleneck at the packaging level in the most cost effective manner, while providing the lowest risk, most flexible development package. To this end, we will present our work on an electrical LGA field replaceable package with optical components. These optical components enable larger I/O bandwidth density between the MCM and PCB than that allowed by a standard electrical package. ©2006 IEEE.

Authors: Fan J.; Drewniak J.L.; Shi H.; Knighten J.L.
Author full names: Fan, Jun (56419124000); Drewniak, James L. (7007149908); Shi, Hao (55360857400); Knighten, James L. (6701536370)
Title: DC power-bus modeling and design with a mixed-potential integral-equation formulation and circuit extraction
Source title: IEEE Transactions on Electromagnetic Compatibility
Abstract: Application of a circuit extraction approach based on a mixed-potential integral equation formulation (CEMPIE) for dc power-bus modeling in high-speed digital designs is detailed herein. Agreement with measurements demonstrates the effectiveness of the approach. Dielectric losses are included into the calculation of Green's functions, and thus, incorporated into the rigorous first principles formulation. A SPICE model is then extracted from the diseretized integral equation. A quasistatic approximation is used for Green's functions to keep the extracted circuit elements frequency independent. Previous work has established a necessary meshing criterion in order to ensure accuracy for a given substrate thickness and dielectric constant to a desired frequency. Several power-bus design issues, such as surface mount decoupling and power-plane segmentation, were investigated using the modeling approach. The results and discussions illustrate the application of the method to dc power-bus design for printed circuit and multi-chip module substrates.
Author Keywords: Circuit extraction; dc power-bus design; Dielectric losses; Mixed-potential integral equation formulation; Segmented power plane; Surface mount decoupling

Title: RF simplifies in-car wireless communications
Source title: Electronics World
Abstract: The wide applications of black and white ceramic the four key areas of automotive design which include power supplies for RF, RF circuit layout, RF boards, and antennas, are discussed. In-car wireless communications is one of the most exciting and rapidly evolving fields in automotive and the prime applications include MP3, gaming and DVD video streaming, in-car digital TV, and Digital Audio Broadcasting (DAB). The active semiconductor devices in in-car RF communication systems amplify any noise in the power supply or signal chain and overlay it onto the desired signal. Circuits detecting high frequencies have special requirements because noise from wanted signals such as that radiated from bus lines can impair functionality. A proper selection of suitable components and off-the-shelf modules that have passed stringent automotive certification would result in the designing of a successful in-car wireless communications solution.

Authors: Arshak K.; Jafer E.
Title: Design of telemetry platform system for biomedical pressure monitoring
Source title: ISSE 2006 - 29th International Spring Seminar on Electronics Technology: Nano Technologies for Electronics Packaging, Conference Proceedings
Abstract: The main goal of this work is to fabricate a miniaturized, low power, bi-directional wireless communication system that can be used for in vivo pressure monitoring. The system prototype consists of miniature FSK transceiver integrated with Microcontroller unit (MCU) in one small package, chip antenna, and capacitive interface circuitry based on Delta-sigma (ΣΔ) modulator. At the base station side, an FSK receiver/transmitter is connected to another MCU unit, which send the received data or received instructions from a PC through a graphical user interface GUI. Industrial, Scientific and Medical (ISM) band RF (433 MHz) was used to achieve half duplex communication between the two sides. A digital filtering has been used in the capacitive interface to reduce noise effects forming capacitance to digital converter (CDC). All the modules of the mixed signal system are integrated in a printed circuit board (PCB) of size 22.46×20.168mm. © 2006 IEEE.

Authors: Meng X.; Zhang Q.; Xing M.; Chu W.

Title: Design of high-speed parallel signal processing board based on ADSP-21160
Source title: Journal of Electronic Measurement and Instrumentation
Abstract: This paper presents a design of high-speed parallel signal processing board based on four ADSP21160 processors for High Frequency Ground Wave Radar (HFGWR) system. The board has 2400MFLOPS of peak processing performance onboard. Using link ports and VMEbus interface to communicate between boards, the board-to-board communications bandwidth is up to 1200 MBytes/s. It has many promising characteristics such as topology flexibility, good scalable capability, high reliability and maintainability. It can be applied to construct an integrated high performance parallel signal processing system. The paper describes high-speed circuit design techniques used to design the Printed Circuit Board (PCB), simulates and analyses signal integrity(SI), ensuring high quality at design.
Author Keywords: ADSP-21160; PCB; Signal processing system

Authors: Aloisio A.; Branchini P.; Cevenini F.; Izzo V.; Loffredo S.; Lomoro R.
Title: Signal integrity and timing issues of VME64x double edge cycles
Source title: IEEE Transactions on Nuclear Science
Abstract: The Double-Edge Source Synchronous Block Transfer (2eSST) is the latest performance update to the VME64 protocol, approved as an ANSI standard in 2003. This extension has taken the VMEs data transfer rate from the original 40 MByte/s to 320 MByte/s. The architectural change at the base of such an impressive step forward is twofold. Different from all the previous cycles, data transfers are driven synchronously by the producer, without handshaking, and data is latched on both the rising and falling edges of the strobe signal. The double edge clocking effectively doubles the bandwidth and it is normally present on PC motherboards equipped with double data rate RAM chips and high-performance graphic adapters. In these applications, a careful approach to signal integrity has shown to be critical in order to avoid timing violations. In parallel, multidrop bus architecture with long lines and up to 21 slots, these concerns become imperative for successful operations. In this paper we present the tests performed on 2eSST. The Motorola MVME6100 and a custom designed board have been used to characterize the timing with different bus loading conditions and to evaluate the impact of different layout choices. Driving capability and crosstalk immunity of enhanced transceivers specifically developed for 2eSST and traditional components are compared.
Author Keywords: Data acquisition; Double data rate; Double edge; Signal integrity

Authors: Kindratenko V.; Pointer D.
Author full names: Kindratenko, Volodymyr (6505973419); Pointer, David (9271987500)
Title: Mapping a sensor interface and a reconfigurable communication system to an FPGA core
Source title: Sensor Letters
Abstract: In this paper, we present a novel approach for integrating a standard sensor interface and a reconfigurable wireless data communication channel on a single Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) chip. In a traditional wireless sensor device, sensor and communication electronics are built as separate components and their integration consists of designing a board to accommodate multiple integrated circuits (ICs). In contrast, the FPGA core allows us to put a standard I2C sensor interface, embedded Digital Signal Processing (DSP) algorithms for Software-Defined Radio (SDR), and a microprocessor control system on a single-chip reconfigurable device. In our experimental FPGA-based sensor platform, the I2C interface is used both to receive data from the temperature sensor and to control the analog Radio Frequency (RF) transceiver board. Amplitude Shift Keying (ASK) modulation and demodulation are implemented using DSP techniques within an SDR framework, and the microprocessor system is used to read sensor data and control various components. The prototype design was deployed on a Nallatech development board containing a Xilinx Virtex 2V3000 FPGA chip and was successfully tested with Dallas Semiconductor DS1721 digital temperature sensor. One instance of the prototype transmitted the temperature red by the sensor while second instance acted upon the received over the air temperature readings by turning LED on or off. Title: Check of Inconsistency of Gun Scale Based on PCL-833

Authors: Regirer S.A.; Shapovalov D.S.
Author full names: Regirer, S.A. (7004544778); Shapovalov, D.S. (6602415693)
Title: Filling Space in Public Transport by Passengers
Source title: Automation and Remote Control
Abstract: Modeling of motional behavior of the passengers in the municipal transport - bus, trolleybus, streetcar, subway, or suburban electric train - was discussed for the first time. Attention was focused on the relations for passenger flow densities that would adequately describe the main characteristics of the averaged passenger behavior and their distribution during boarding, travel, and exit. Besides studying the passenger flows and observance of schedules, these models could be used to predict the degree of bus filling, estimate the comfort level, and work out recommendations for bus configurations.

Authors: Homem M.T.; Pignède M.; Merri M.; Reggestad V.; Pidgeon A.; Matussi S.
Author full names: Homem, Miguel Terra (55885947200); Pignède, Max (55886055600); Merri, Mario (6603356650); Reggestad, Vemund (9732471700); Pidgeon, Alastair (9734985500); Matussi, Sandro (6508186258)
Title: The GALILEO simulator: A major step in software technology from single spacecraft to constellation simulators
Source title: SpaceOps 2006 Conference
Abstract: In the European GALILEO in-orbit validation (IOV) program one essential element in the Galileo Ground Control Segment (GCS) is the Satellite Constellation Simulator (CSIM). The role of CSIM is to provide a complete and reliable environment which will play a key role in the validation of the GCS and in particular in the validation of the Satellite Constellation Control Facility (SCCF). Further to this validation of GCS computer systems it will also be used extensively by the IOV operations staff; first during the operations preparation activities, i.e. to train the Galileo Flight Control Team (FCT) and to validate the Flight Operations Procedures (FOPs); then during the actual in-orbit operations, e.g. to validate on-board software related modifications (e.g. patches validation prior to actual upload in a given spacecraft); finally in the investigation of anomalies. The main technical challenge for CSIM is being able to run multiple spacecraft models and being able to do so in a globally coordinated fashion: CSIM must not only be able to cope with several satellites but it must also be able to represent correctly that those satellites form a constellation delivering a unified service whereby each satellite or ground station model is executed in its own process but controlled by a central simulation environment. CSIM is required to provide a coherent representation of the constellation and the associated ground stations. Last but not least at any given point in time CSIM must be able to cope with "differing" satellites in the sense that they may run different on-board software versions, independent models, activate specific states, be driven by different databases, and so on. This paper will explain with some details the software problems to cope with in order to fulfill the functionalities expected from CSIM. The paper will also be the opportunity to present the latest stages achieved effectively in the on-going implementation phase (year 2006 is a crucial milestone of the whole Galileo program). The technical considerations in the paper will address how CSIM is organized on a multi-processor and multi-machine server-client distributed scalable architecture with some centralized kernel processes. There are also a significant number of ground connections (of different type) to take into account. It will also explore how processing and/or memory bottlenecks can be minimized (e.g. regarding the various emulators required to execute the real on-board software with the required fidelity) and how the expected demanding performance can be achieved. Indeed the scale of the systems at hand is not small: the number of spacecrafts in the constellation is 27. At any one time there may be 6 orbital spares. A further 18 spacecrafts are required for refurbishment and growth. This means that CSIM is required to handle at least 30 (up to 51) different spacecrafts, their orbits and associated databases and on-board software images. Each spacecraft simulated is required to provide its own breakpoint capability independently of the other satellite simulated. CSIM will use also Just-in-time compilation technology whereby significant gain in performance is being investigated to allow high fidelity models to be provided for all the spacecraft in a constellation, not just those in-contact or coming into contact with the ground. CSIM is based on the SuSe LINUX platforms. The paper will conclude by presenting the forthcoming CSIM milestones and by broadening the software technological challenges over such a world size project which Europe with Galileo is undertaking. © 2006 by ESA.

Title: Research and prototype implementation of a TCP/IP offload engine based on the ML403 xilinx development board
Source title: Proceedings - 2006 International Conference on Information and Communication Technologies: From Theory to Applications, ICTTA 2006
Abstract: Purpose-to remove CPU from heavy services of protocol processing, and alleviate the bottlenecks of communication system to suit for the high speed network. Methodology-by analysis and design with Linux specialties binding to functions of ML403 development version, to code or modify portion of kernel code and use VHDL to design the hardware section. Result-by analysis the design requirements of TCPIIP offload, to simplify the protocol stack of TCPIIP, and finally to give out a ML403 based solution for TOE architecture design, to build a system experiment platform and last we draw some conclusions and some test results. Conclusion-Although the results show that the performance improving is not much, the simple success of test indicates that this solution is correct and potential. It will contribute to the performance improvement of whole communication system and popularization to the TOE network card. © 2006 IEEE.

Authors: Lück T.; Göhler E.; Bodenbach M.; Winkel J.; Förster F.
Author full names: Lück, Thorsten (13410229900); Göhler, Eckart (16230051500); Bodenbach, Michael (13409553600); Winkel, Jón (8611673400); Förster, Frank (56781090700)
Title: The GATE receiver - A full-scale galileo/GPS monitor receiver
Source title: Proceedings of the Institute of Navigation - 19th International Technical Meeting of the Satellite Division, ION GNSS 2006
Abstract: For the purpose of pre Galileo system verification and testing, the Galileo Test Environment (GATE) is setup in the German Alps to reproduce a realistic test bed for the Galileo satellite navigation system. In fact, a complete miniature navigation system is built up consisting of a control, ground and pseudo-space segment. For system monitoring and testing a receiver is required, which is capable of processing all signals specified in the Galileo system specification. To prove interoperability and for reference purposes the receiver will also process Galileo and GPS signals on L1 in a common processing chain. This paper describes a modular receiver design, developed for the use as a user receiver as well as a system monitor receiver. Detailed results from performance tests will be presented. Up to three single band receivers with radio frequency front-end and base band processor occupy up to nine slots of the PXI framework to serve any of the Galileo radio frequency bands E5, E6 and L1. One base-band board and a front-end system consisting of two cPCI boards cover each frequency band. The front-end system consists of a digital signal conditioning board and an analog front-end board. As the base-band units are based on field programmable gate arrays (FPGA), the actual band specific functionality of the receiver is implemented in a HDL and uploaded to the system. This flexibility allows all base-band units to be designed identically. The three receiver front-ends similarly have an identical PCB-layout, which reduces costs. The digital signal conditioning boards are all identical. The analog front-end boards have identical PCB layout, but differ in the components fitted (filters, LO-frequencies). Receiving the whole E5 band (i.e. E5a and E5b) including the first side-lobe (71 MHz) through one front-end system is the single most challenging requirement on the front-end system. To fulfill the required amplitude and group delay flatness in the pass-band is very challenging. The very high bandwidth demands high performance components and a careful design. For the other two bands the bandwidth is more relaxed. All three front-ends have a low-IF architecture with a single analog mixer stage and different filter stages in the RF- and IF-domain, respectively. For the subsequent A/D-converter jitter is a major concern. The sampling clock must exhibit ultra low jitter in order to prevent degradation of the received signal. The digitized signal is converted to base-band using a digital I/Q down-converter, thus the data rate to the digital base-band board is halved and the input bit-width is doubled. The advantage is that the requirements on the clocking of the base-band board are relaxed. Selection of the band to serve is performed by software, which uploads the corresponding configuration file to the base band FPGA. Two gate arrays of the latest Virtex 4 family are used for the base band processing. They provide up to thirty channels with up to five correlators each, controlled by embedded micro controllers (IBM PowerPC). Thus the receiver supports 90 generic channels, 30 on each frequency. For AltBOC tracking two channels are slaved together resulting in a maximum of 15 AltBOC channels simultaneously. Both gate array and associated micro-controller can be configured independently within the same RF band allowing to track GPS and Galileo/GATE signals simultaneously on one base band board. Different tracking methods for BOC, Alt-BOC signals or combined in phase and quadrature phase signal tracking algorithms are also implemented. All base band boards use the same clock signal provided by a rear PXI backplane mounted oscillator. The oscillator module can be either a rubidium or a temperature compensated crystal oscillator (TCXO) module depending on the application and requirements. Making use of dedicated clock lines of the PXI backplane, the clock signal is distributed to all receivers providing coherent clocking of all processing modules. To synchronize the local clocks of all receivers, a specialized PXI line is used to distribute a central signal, which triggers the pseudo range measurement on all receiver boards. Using a dedicated eight-bit bus for PXI cross-slot communication and the PXI star trigger lines, the local clocks of all boards are synchronized to each other. Each receiver board is addressable through the PXI bus. The main controller of each board is embedded in a fourth FPGA, running a Linux operating system. This offers most flexibility and allows addressing and configuring the receiver using standard protocols as TCP/IP or even HTTP and XML. Detailed results with real GPS signals as well as simulated Galileo signals from the GATE transmitters will be presented, focusing on acquisition and tracking methods and performance for new Galileo signal structures.

Authors: Thürey S.
Author full names: Thürey, Stefan (8974628100)
Title: Data management for the Herschel and Planck spacecraft - Considerations for future missions
Source title: European Space Agency, (Special Publication) ESA SP
Abstract: 1. The Herschel and Planck Scientific Satellites The Herschel and Planck satellites are currently in development at ESA and European industry for a launch in 2007. They the most advanced and complex scientific astronomy missions ESA has conducted, carrying cryogenic payloads, which are sensitive in the far infrared and sub-millimeter range of the electromagnetic spectrum. Both spacecraft have a high degree of autonomy including failure-recovery capabilities for continuing the nominal mission. 2. Architecture and Design Drivers of the On-board Avionics 2.1. Key Requirements The on-board Data Management Subsystem has a common architecture for the two satellites and is in charge of all data communication tasks and is controlling all Service Module (SVM) subsystems. Also for the Attitude Control and Measurement Subsystem (ACMS) of the two spacecraft the same on-board computer and interface approach could be utilized, achieving a high degree of commonality, as required by ESA. The paper addresses requirements and design considerations, which are relevant for the on-board avionics of a wide range of spacecraft to be developed in the European context. Main purpose of the DMS is to ensure, that the primary product of a scientific space mission becomes available on ground, i.e. the data from the instrument payload. Therefore, a high degree of adaptability and flexibility for these data, throughout all phases of a space project is apparently desirable, high volumes of data need to be processed, but some temporary degradation may be tolerable. However, design-drivers for the Avionics Subsystem are determined by the task of "controlling the spacecraft". This is even more the case for highly integrated control and data systems, which make use of a single (redundant) on-board computer and associated communication infrastructure for attitude control, control of the rest of the spacecraft subsystems, and supervision and data processing and routing for the payload elements. Within such an architecture, the dominating features for hardware, software, and interfaces are: relatively small data rates needed for control tasks, simplicity and robustness, guaranteed deterministic behavior and timing, complete testability, and a 100% guarantee for functionality and performance as needed for spacecraft control. These requirements are obviously in conflict with desires for flexibility and variability for payload data processing. As a consequence, payload data handling must be of secondary importance in such an architecture. Payload data handling can be accommodated within an integrated data management architecture, however only in free architectural and performance "niches". Payload-related requirements should be accepted and implemented only after having demonstrated that spacecraft control can run unaffected in all operational cases. They should never be the drivers for a certain avionics architecture used for spacecraft control. If, however, payload-related requirements are incompatible with a simple and robust avionics architecture, one way out is an independent processor- and communications- infrastructure, which is devoted to on-board payload processing. 2.2. Avionics Architecture The on-board avionics architecture of Herschel and Planck has been specified and designed in line with these considerations. During early phases (feasibility studies, phase A) of this ESA-project, the scientists had all needed flexibility to define the characteristics of their scientific data and their operational needs. After reviewing their inputs from the scientific and engineering point of view, agreements were reached at the beginning of project-phase B about significant data reductions within the instruments (powers of 10), adequate instrument-internal buffering, and simplification of operations of instruments. Data handling problems and complexity were solved at the source, and the resulting functional and performance characteristics of the data and control interfaces could be implemented without difficulties, at moderate cost, and with guaranteed performance to the full satisfaction of the scientists, although the related requirements may look rather restrictive and conservative. On the other hand, a spacecraft-level avionics architecture could be specified by ESA, and designed and developed by industry, which is in line with the considerations above and represents the state of the art of spacecraft electronics design. It fulfils so far our expectations and is capable to handle all tasks needed for controlling highly complex space missions. In the following, selected key features will be discussed in more detail in order to highlight characteristics, which are important on spacecraft- and mission-level. Figure 1 depicts a block diagram of the on-board avionics on spacecraft-level, including the ACMS. Main characteristics are utilization of two redundant computers with a common architecture, and common basic software services and operating system. This approach has resulted in benefits in several areas for ESA. On the other hand, this approach was allowing ESA to delegate full subsystem responsibility for DMS and ACMS to different groups of European subcontractors, also seen as advantage from ESA's view. Saab Ericson Space is the subcontractor for the CDMUs and ACCs and the Basic Software. These on-board computers have been described in detail in a paper presented during DASIA 2004, Ref [1]. Alenia is in charge for the SVMs of the two satellites, including their DMS and its spacecraft-level application-SW, whereas Dutch Space is the subcontractor for the ACMS including SW. Overall industrial prime for the Herschel and Planck mission is Alcatel Space, Cannes. Among others they are in charge of ensuring commonality in hardware and software. A further common characteristics are data busses according to MIL-Std. 1553B for DMS and for ACMS, together with the same basic features for data transfer. This results among others in benefits during interface testing and spacecraft-level verification. table presented 3. Specific Features of the On-board Avionics The paper will further discuss certain important mission-level requirements and resulting specific characteristics of the avionics architecture. Data processing space- to- ground: (Telemetry) - Acquiring digitized data from several subsystems and instruments, like housekeeping/status- data and science-data, with guaranteed reliability and data-volumes. - Precision-time-tagging these data, and storing all data for later-on retrieval - mainly to cover periods of no ground-contact. Data processing ground- to- space: (Telecommanding) - Detection, Decoding and Distribution of Telecommand messages from the Transponder, such that they can be executed error-free, in sequence, without duplications and omissions. - Storing of Telecommands, which shall be executed during times without ground-contact, releasing them on-time, and routing them to end-users. - Guaranteed commanding-access to certain essential functions of the satellite via hardwired command paths. Main on-board task: Spacecraft Control - Running of control loops for nominal Subsystem-Control - Failure Detection, Isolation, and Recovery - FDIR with: - Monitoring of selected parameters against configurable thresholds, - Evaluation of Event-packets generated by other on-board users, - and taking adequate action in case something is non-nominal. - Autonomous recovery from an anomaly, or reconfiguration of redundancies of the satellites, during periods without ground contact, in order maintain nominal operations of the S/C and instruments. The ACMS is in charge of its own FDIR, covering the ACC, attitude sensors and actuators. Safeguard Memory: The CDMU, or the ACMS, is keeping a record of the configuration of all on-board units in a hot-redundant, non-volatile memory (SafeGuard Memory, 512 kBytes). This SGM is independent from the memory of the Processor Module. The configuration data consist of On/Off-status, health-status, etc. for each unit. The data are used and updated, if any reconfiguration on unit- to S/C-level needs to be carried out (autonomously). Also, a Critical Event Log is kept there. This feature and its robust architecture is considered essential for spacecraft control, however the usefulness for the instruments is very limited. Solid State Mass Memory: The SSMM is capable to store all on-board data for two days, 24 Gigabits max. On one PCS 3 sections of 8 Gbits are powered, while a fourth section can replace any failed one (3-out-of-4-redundancy, to guarantee End-of-Life-performance). Additionally, the CDMU contains a complete, redundant SSMM-module. As one of the rare cases, where payload requirements were direct driver for the DMS architecture, the overall size of this SSMM is determined by scientific needs. For highly reliable storing of crucial data like the MTL and OBCPs, it has been decided to operate this SSMM in hot redundancy, and as a by-product, also all scientific data are well protected against losses during downlinking. What concerns the control-software for the mass memory, a complex file management system is considered unnecessary, neither for spacecraft- nor for payload-data. Realtime Operating System: Based on certain criteria, industry selected RTEMS, an open-source product, in a common configuration for CDMUs and ACCs. ESA is stressing the need to validate this software according to ESA-rules with scrutiny, as part of the industrial contract. Satellite Data Bus Protocol: Another common feature is the Herschel/Planck-specific Satellite Data Bus Protocol used on the 1553 data busses. It is characterized by simplicity and a guaranteed decoupling of data traffic related to spacecraft control from instrument data. As a side effect, also each instrument has a guarantee, never to encounter bottlenecks in competition with other instruments. 4. Recommendations for Future Missions, Conclusions.

Authors: Hobbs J.M.; Windlass H.; Sundaram V.; Chun S.; White G.E.; Swaminathan M.; Tummala R.R.
Author full names: Hobbs, Joseph M. (7202114500); Windlass, Hitesh (6506311024); Sundaram, Venky (7005413692); Chun, Sungjun (7202148413); White, George E. (56222983300); Swaminathan, Madhavan (7103353366); Tummala, Rao R. (34573915900)
Title: Simultaneous switching noise suppression for high speed systems using embedded decoupling
Source title: Proceedings - Electronic Components and Technology Conference
Abstract: As part of the System on a Package (SOP) concept being developed at the Packaging Research Center (PRC), Georgia Tech, a test vehicle to demonstrate the suppression of simultaneous switching noise (SSN) using embedded decoupling capacitors is being implemented. This test vehicle uses thin film sequential buildup technology on a low-cost organic platform incorporating polymer-ceramic nanocomposite dielectrics. This paper presents the design, fabrication and validation of embedded decoupling for SOP technology.
